overview: The Qutb Shahi sultanate grew from a Bahmani province into a major eastern Deccan kingdom, based at Golconda and later Hyderabad. Its usual dynastic dates are 1518-1687. The imported 1492-1700 map extends beyond these dates: early outlines approximate the regional core, while the final snapshot includes substantial southern expansion.

sections.title: A kingdom, a new capital and royal families

items.text: Sultan Quli rose in Bahmani service to govern Telangana. As that larger state weakened, his authority developed into the Qutb Shahi dynasty, conventionally dated from 1518. Fortifying Golconda and extending control over surrounding territories helped turn a provincial base into a kingdom.

Before becoming ruler in 1550, Ibrahim Quli had found refuge at Vijayanagara after his brother took power. Back at Golconda, he supported Telugu poetry and Persian literature. Political borders did not prevent people, languages and artistic interests from travelling between courts.

Relations with Vijayanagara later deteriorated. Ibrahim joined the Deccan coalition that defeated Rama Raya’s forces at Talikota in 1565. The victorious sultanates soon quarrelled again: cooperation against a shared enemy did not turn their separate kingdoms into a permanent alliance.

Hayat Bakshi Begum connected three reigns: she was a ruler’s daughter, another ruler’s wife and Abdullah Qutb Shah’s mother. When her son inherited as a minor, she exercised political authority as regent. Her imposing tomb matches her husband’s in scale, making her importance visible in the landscape.

sections.title: Building a city people could live in

items.text: Crowding and unreliable water at Golconda helped prompt the foundation of Hyderabad in 1591. The new city stood beside the Musi River on the route to Masulipatnam. Moving the court also created room for officials, soldiers and the population overflowing the old fortified settlement.

The Charminar marked Hyderabad’s main crossroads. Its upper floor included a mosque, while spiral stairs ran inside the four minarets. It was both a striking landmark and part of a working city plan, helping organize movement through the new capital.

Planners placed tanks and orchards in low ground where they could collect runoff, with palaces on nearby hills. Water management shaped the city’s gardens. A beautiful view depended partly on knowing where rainwater would go.

The surviving Qutb Shahi hammam contains interconnected cisterns and channels for hot and cold water. Its rooms formed a carefully supplied bathing complex. Conservators have questioned the old assumption that it served only funeral washing, suggesting a functioning bathhouse instead; its exact use remains debated.

During recent conservation, workers removed modern roof concrete and uncovered terracotta pipes feeding the hammam’s cisterns. They also found historic aqueducts beside the building. Those discoveries let researchers trace real water routes, rather than guessing from the appearance of the rooms.

sections.title: Healthcare, crafts and things people used

items.text: Muhammad Quli founded the Darushifa hospital in 1595. Architectural documentation records patient chambers around a stone-paved courtyard, with a bath, mosque and lodging complex. Its riverbank setting and fragrant surroundings belonged to historical ideas about healing. Buildings preserve evidence of organized care even where individual patients’ stories are missing.

A small jade mortar and pestle in New Delhi’s National Museum resembles a familiar tool for grinding herbs and spices, but its costly material and gold-filled inscription suggest royal ownership. The museum dates it to the seventeenth century and connects it with Muhammad Qutb Shah.

The same mortar preserves Persian writing in Nastaliq script. In the museum’s Roman transcription, “Banda-i-khaksar Muhammad Qutb Shah” means “the humblest man, Mohammad Qutb Shah.” This is a surviving ruler’s inscription, presented here in transcription; the modest wording sits on a decidedly luxurious grinding tool.

A cotton cover attributed to Golconda around 1640-1650 shows courtly figures in Persian and Indian dress. Its colours were created through mordant painting and dyeing, alongside resist dyeing. Skilled clothmakers combined drawing with knowledge of how fibres and dyes behaved.

A note on that cover records an inventory at Amber Palace in late 1673. The cloth therefore preserves two kinds of history: the scenes its maker painted and the later bookkeeping of its owners. A storeroom clerk’s small annotation helps trace an object’s travels.

Masulipatnam’s textile trade drew on surrounding weaving villages. Local chaya root supplied a valued dye for patterned cotton. Cloth exported from the port linked farming, colouring, weaving and merchant work across the region.

A painting made at Golconda around 1630 shows Sultan Abdullah with attendants, dancers and musicians. The vizier seated beside him helps museum researchers identify its early-reign setting. It offers a carefully arranged image of court entertainment, rather than a picture of every family’s leisure.

Excavators found granite enclosure-wall foundations around Sultan Quli’s tomb. This evidence changed the picture of the monument: it had stood within a formal garden rather than simply alone in an open landscape. Archaeology can recover the missing setting around a familiar building.

Muhammad Qutb Shah’s mausoleum once carried glazed tiles. Removing modern cement revealed original fragments and patterns on its dome and other surfaces. Conservators retained those fragments while adding newly made tiles where evidence allowed restoration. The brilliant green surface combines surviving old work with documented modern repair.

ending.text: Aurangzeb’s Mughal conquest in 1687 ended Qutb Shahi sovereignty. Hyderabad lost its role as the regional capital, but its communities and buildings continued; the Mughals completed the Mecca Mosque. The map’s 1700 endpoint is later coverage, not an extra thirteen years of independent Qutb Shahi rule.
